of immunodeficiency, such as hypogammaglobulinemia or 
altered B‑cell development (14).
Environmental factors. There are several dietary, lifestyle 
and environmental factors that have been linked to RA; 
however, tobacco exposure is the key factor. Numerous 
studies have discovered odds ratios of links between smoking 
and RA, and it is estimated that 20‑30% of risk factors for 
RA involve exposure to smoke. However, there are a number 
of aspects of the smoking‑RA association that may act as 
mediators of the elevated risk for the development of RA. 
The main finding is that smoking is most strongly linked 
to ACPA‑positive RA, particularly when the SE is present. 
Furthermore, even when RA is not present, smoking has 
long been linked to the occurrence of RF. The implication 
is that RA may be caused by biologic interactions among 
these variables. Although there are numerous other local and 
systemic effects of tobacco use that may affect immunity, it 
has been suggested that smoking may increase citrullination, 
which, in the presence of the proper genetic background, 
results in the presentation of citrullinated proteins and the 
generation of ACPA (15). In addition to exposure to tobacco 
smoke, numerous studies have consistently revealed a link 
between occupational silica/dust exposure and RA, specifi‑
cally ACPA‑positive RA (16). The risk of RA has also been 
disparately associated with a number of dietary or other 
factors, including supplements or drugs (17). These include 
a higher risk of developing RA due to a decreased intake of 
vitamin D and antioxidants and a higher diet intake of sugar, 
sodium, red meat, protein and iron. Additionally, in the 
FDRs of RA patients who did not have classifiable RA at the 
time of the study, the self‑reported consumption of omega‑3 
fatty acid supplements and fatty acid biomarkers revealed 
that higher blood levels of fatty acids and increased intake 
were linked to a lower risk of RF and ACPA positivity (18). 
Furthermore, the risk of RA has been linked to healthy life‑
styles, such as a lower body mass index and healthier diets 
that are generally high in fruits, whole grains, and vegetables 
and low in sugar and animal fats, but these definitions vary 
throughout research (19). Laragione et al (20) examined 
the effects of a high‑magnesium diet in two distinct mouse 
models of collagen‑induced arthritis and RA induced with 
KRN serum. The high‑magnesium diet group was notably 
protected with decreased joint damage and arthritis severity, 
as well as the decreased expression of IL‑1β, IL‑6 and 
TNF‑α. Additionally, the high‑magnesium group had higher 
numbers of Foxp3+ Treg cells and IL‑10‑producing T‑cells. 
They represent a new role for magnesium in suppressing 
arthritis, in expanding Foxp3+ T reg cells, and in the produc‑
tion of IL‑10, and demonstrate that these effects are mediated 
by the intestinal microbiome. Their findings suggest a novel 
approach to altering the intestinal microbiome to treat RA 
and other autoimmune and inflammatory diseases (20).
Immune system dysregulation. Immune system dysregulation 
plays a central role in the etiology of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), 
which is an autoimmune disease characterized by chronic 
inflammation and joint destruction. The immune system fails 
to distinguish self from non‑self, leading to the recognition 
of self‑antigens as foreign. Proteins modified by citrullina‑
tion (conversion of arginine to citrulline) are misidentified as 
threats. This results in the development of autoantibodies, such 
as RF and ACPAs, which are hallmarks of RA. Dysregulated 
immune cells release excessive pro‑inflammatory cytokines, 
including TNF‑α, IL‑1β and IL‑6. This affects the recruitment 
of inflammatory cells (e.g., macrophages and neutrophils) 
and increases synovial inflammation and hyperplasia (pannus 
formation). Immune dysregulation leads to the chronic inflam‑
mation of the synovial membrane. Proliferating synovial tissue 
invades cartilage and bone, which causes bone resorption in 
which osteoclast activation by cytokines [e.g., receptor acti‑
vator of NF‑κB ligand (RANKL)] leads to bone erosion (21).
As one of the main pro‑inflammatory cytokines in RA, 
TNF‑α, has been shown to increase inflammation by upregu‑
lating TNFR II, activating the NF‑κB pathway, and causing 
RA‑fibroblast‑like synoviocytes (FLS) to secrete RANKL 
for osteoclast formation. Likewise, in RA, macrophages 
are the primary source of IL‑1, which triggers potent and 
rapid inflammatory reactions. Furthermore, RA is partially 
caused by chemokines, including IL‑8, monocyte chemoat‑
tractant protein‑1 and C‑X‑C motif ligand 13, as well as other 
inflammatory factors, such as IL‑12, IL‑15, IL‑18, IL‑32 and 
granulocyte‑macrophage colony‑stimulating factor. These 
cytokines contribute to the pathogenic inflammatory environ‑
ment within the synovium by forming a complex network with 
one another, even though they cannot directly cause RA (22).
3. Diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis
The early diagnosis and identification of short‑term inflamma‑
tory arthritis that progresses to chronic RA in the future can 
be challenging in normal clinical procedures. More patients 
with inflammatory arthritis have a moderate‑to‑high disease 
activity, and some experience aggressive joint deterioration 
and systemic consequences, compared to a small number 
of patients who may experience spontaneous remission and 
others who may have a mild disease history with slow progres‑
sion. Consequently, there is a need for imaging evaluations 
and/or laboratory biomarkers that would be more useful in the 
early detection of illness.
The American College of Rheumatology (ACR)/European 
League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) categorisation criteria 
for RA included acute phase reactants and ACPAs, particu‑
larly at elevated levels, which are linked to aggressive illness. 
The revised classification criteria for RA were established by 
the ACR and the EULAR in 2010. These criteria replaced the 
older 1987 ACR criteria to improve the early diagnosis and 
classification of RA. This system assigns a score from 0 to 
10, with a score of ≥6 classifying a patient as having definite 
RA (23). Therefore, meeting these requirements encourages 
doctors to begin the right treatment as soon as possible to 
prevent irreparable harm. To further enhance the diagnosis of 
RA, novel biomarkers are still required, even with the high 
diagnostic value of RFs and ACPAs. Recently, a number of new

help with early diagnosis and forecast the future progression 
of the disease. Imaging methods, particularly ultrasound (US), 
may enhance the early detection of RA in addition to clinical 
symptoms and serological testing, particularly in individuals 
who test negative for the disease (24).
High resolution multiplanar images of soft tissue, carti‑
lage and bone profiles can be obtained using US. The early 
diagnosis and monitoring of chronic arthritis can benefit from 
the careful evaluation of the smallest structural changes made 
possible by the high resolution of the most recent generation 
of US technology. The extent and distribution of the different 
characteristics of cartilage degradation can be thoroughly 
analysed using US. The most striking illustration of the devas‑
tation that chronic arthritis can cause is bone erosions. Due to 
the high sensitivity of US, bone erosions as minimal as a tenth 
of a millimetre can be found. The most sensitive morpholog‑
ical biomarkers to forecast the occurrence of erosions later on 
are most likely the loss of sharpness and subtle abnormalities 
of the bone pattern at the points to interact with the synovial 
pannus (25).
For the diagnosis of RA, the most specific serological indi‑
cators are ACPAs. According to recent research, the ACPA 
responses of patients with RA vary widely and are polyclonal. 
Enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) detect and measure immuno‑
logic reactions by using the catalytic properties of enzymes. 
One heterogeneous EIA method used in clinical analyses is the 
enzyme‑linked immunosorbent test (ELISA). One of the reac‑
tion's components is covalently or nonspecifically adsorbed 
to the surface of a solid phase, like a plastic bead, magnetic 
particle, or microtiter well, in this kind of test. The separa‑
tion of bound and free‑labeled reactants is made easier by this 
connection (26). The basis of gene microarray technology is 
the capacity to deposit a wide variety of DNA sequences on 
a tiny surface, often a glass slide (commonly called a ‘chip’). 
The various DNA fragments are grouped in rows and columns 
so that each fragment's identification may be determined by 
where it is located on the array (27).
A variety of analytical methods based on ELISA and 
microarray technologies have been used so far, allowing for 
the accurate early detection of RA due to its diverse response. 
As regards the former, an ELISA technique was created based 
on chimeric fibrin/filaggrin synthetic peptide that is extremely 
sensitive and specific for RA detection when compared to 
healthy controls and those with other chronic illnesses (28).
Following this technological requirement, the 
development of electrochemical immunosensors using 
nanostructured materials, specifically, multiwalled carbon 
nanotube (MWCNT)‑polymer composites, offers the potential 
for the creation of low‑cost, high‑sensitivity point‑of‑care 
diagnostic devices when certain biomarkers are available, as 
in this instance. This makes use of a quartz crystal microbal‑
ance that has been altered by carbon nanotubes (CNTs), which 
have been further coated with a synthetic peptide receptor (29). 
Additionally, a citrullinated specific peptide receptor and 
a MWCNT‑polystyrene (PS) composite transducer are used 
to create a basic electrochemical immunosensor. Rabbit sera 
that had already received the citrullinated peptide vaccina‑
tion were used to evaluate the performance of the device, and 
human sera from patients with RA were used for additional 
testing. The advantages of this method are demonstrated by 
its simplicity in transducer manufacture, covalent modifica‑
tion with the peptide receptor, miniaturisation, and need for 
inexpensive, basic equipment (30).
4. Pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis
The pathogenesis of RA involves complex interactions within 
the immune system, leading to chronic inflammation and joint 
damage. RA is considered an autoimmune disease, meaning 
that the immune system mistakenly targets and attacks the 
body's own tissues, particularly the synovium (lining of the 
joints) (31). The exact trigger for this autoimmune response 
is not yet fully understood, although it is believed to involve 
a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental 
factors. It has been shown that immunological activities, 
known as the ‘pre‑RA phase’, may take place years before 
signs of joint inflammation become apparent. Peptide arginine 
deiminases performs a post‑translational alteration known as 
citrullination on these proteins containing arginine residues, 
converting them to citrulline (32). Furthermore, cytokine 
release that may result in joint inflammation and modified 
self‑antigens can be triggered by joint abnormalities, such as 
synovial hyperplasia or synovial infections (33). Citrullinated 
proteins (vimentin, type II collagen, histones, fibrin, fibro‑
nectin, Epstein‑Barr nuclear antigen 1 and α‑enolase) are no 
longer recognised by the immune system as self‑structures 
because of the susceptibility genes HLA‑DR1 and HLA‑DR4. 
Antigen‑presenting cells are activated dendritic cells that take 
up antigens in order to start an immune response (34). The 
entire complex moves to the lymph node, where CD4+ helper 
T‑cell activation occurs. Moreover, B‑cells in the germinal 
centre of the lymph node are stimulated by T‑cells in a 
reciprocating and sequential signalling mechanism known as 
co‑stimulation (35).
The human leukocyte antigen D‑related B1 gene 
(HLA‑DRB1) is the most relevant disease‑susceptible gene 
according to genome‑wide analysis of single nucleotide 
polymorphisms in rheumatoid arthritis patients. Other 
disease‑susceptible genes were also found. TNF‑α‑induced 
protein 3, cytotoxic T‑lymphocyte antigen‑4, signal transducer 
and activator of transcription (STAT)4, C‑C motif chemokine 
ligand 21 and peptidyl arginine deiminase 4 are among these 
genes. ACPAs are extremely associated with this particular 
disease, and in individuals who test positive for anti‑CCP 
antibodies, a breakdown of bone or cartilage is more likely to 
develop (36).
On the other hand, common environmental factors, 
including smoking, gingivitis and gut bacterial flora can alter 
the epigenome and demethylate DNA and histones, which 
triggers the production of pro‑inflammatory cytokines (37). 
Air pollution, which is defined as a mixture of gases (nitrates, 
ozone, sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide) and suspended 
particulate materials (PMs) of different sizes, has recently 
drawn increased attention to the field of RA. Air pollution 
may play a role in the aetiology of RA through a few different 
molecular pathways. Inhaled PM can produce free reactive 
oxygen species (ROS) that can trigger NF‑κB), which in turn 
triggers T‑helper cell type 1 (Th1) to release IL‑1 and IL‑6, as 
well as ΤNF‑α. These cytokines stimulate resting monocytes

Для ранней диагностики РА важны автоантигены и антитела, а также методы визуализации, такие как ультразвук (УЗИ), который позволяет выявлять минимальные изменения в тканях и костях. Серологические индикаторы, такие как антитела к циклическим цитруллинированным пептидам (ACPA), являются специфичными для РА. Технологии ELISA и микрочипы позволяют точно диагностировать РА на ранних стадиях. Разрабатываются также электрохимические иммуносенсоры с использованием наноматериалов для создания доступных диагностических устройств.

Патогенез РА связан с аутоиммунными реакциями, приводящими к хроническому воспалению и повреждению суставов. Генетическая предрасположенность и внешние факторы, такие как курение и инфекции, играют роль в развитии заболевания. Ген HLA-DRB1 и другие гены связаны с восприимчивостью к РА. Экологические факторы, включая загрязнение воздуха, могут влиять на эпигеном и способствовать воспалительным процессам через образование реактивных кислородных видов и активацию иммунных клеток.

cells provide auto‑antigens to self‑reactive T‑lymphocytes, 
triggering the latter to migrate to target tissues and enhance 
joint inflammation. Furthermore, ROS contribute in the citrul‑
lination of arginine amino acid residues into citrullinated 
peptides, hence promoting systemic inflammation and chronic 
lung disease. Biochemical events produce ACPAs, which bind 
to cellular Fc receptors and activate complement to initiate an 
immune response that causes bone degradation and inflamma‑
tion in the joints (38).
In RA, the synovium, which lines the joints, becomes 
inflamed due to the increased presence of immune cells and 
inflammatory cytokines. Inflammation in the synovium leads 
to the release of enzymes, such as matrix metalloproteinases, 
which contribute to the degradation of cartilage and bone (39). 
Chronic inflammation results in the formation of a thickened 
layer of synovial tissue (pannus). Pannus invades and erodes 
the cartilage and bone within the joint, causing structural 
damage. The ongoing inflammatory process, combined with 
the action of enzymes and cytokines, leads to the destruction 
of cartilage, bone, and other joint structures. Joint damage 
contributes to pain, swelling, and loss of function. In addi‑
tion to joint involvement, RA can have systemic effects, 
affecting other organs and tissues. Systemic inflammation 
may contribute to conditions, such as rheumatoid nodules, 
vasculitis, and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (40). 
RA is a chronic condition characterized by persistent inflam‑
mation, with periods of exacerbation (flares) and remission. 
The chronic nature of the disease can lead to cumulative joint 
damage over time if not effectively managed (41) (Fig. 2).
5. Therapeutic approaches for rheumatoid arthritis
The therapeutic approaches for RA aim to reduce inflamma‑
tion, alleviate symptoms, attenuate joint damage and improve 
the overall quality of life of patients. The main goal of treating 
RA is to inhibit the disease and induce remission as soon 
as possible after diagnosis, ideally before joint destruction 
occurs (42). The non‑pharmacological approaches aim to 
decrease the level of pain, reduce depression and anxiety and 
enhance mobility. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) have 
gained increasing attention in the field of depression and 
anxiety. Docosahexaenoic acid and eicosapentaenoic acid in 
the series of omega‑3 fatty acids are the two components of 
PUFAs which have been examined for their anti‑depressant 
properties and also to minimize anxiety (43). Other helpful 
measures include surgery, physical therapy, occupational 
therapy and rest. Joint surgery is limited to the most advanced

Хроническое воспаление вызывает образование утолщенного слоя синовиальной ткани (паннуса), который разрушает суставные структуры, вызывая боль, отек и потерю функции. РА также может иметь системные эффекты, влияя на другие органы и повышая риск сердечно-сосудистых заболеваний. Основная цель лечения РА — уменьшение воспаления, облегчение симптомов и предотвращение разрушения суставов. Терапия включает медикаментозные и немедикаментозные подходы, такие как использование полиненасыщенных жирных кислот для снижения депрессии и тревожности, а также хирургическое вмешательство, физиотерапию и отдых.

joints function again (44).
The novel treatment alternatives have been successful in 
minimising symptoms, delaying the course of the condition 
and averting consequences. Non‑steroidal anti‑inflammatory 
drug (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, cyclooxygenase (COX)‑2 
inhibitors and naproxen, are used in the acute phase response 
to lower inflammation and therefore discomfort. The pharma‑
cological effects of NSAIDs are mediated through inhibition 
of COX, namely COX‑2, the levels of which are increased 
during inflammation (45).
Although the suppression of prostaglandins may result 
in severe adverse effects, such as bleeding, gastrointestinal 
ulcers, renal failure, heart failure, rashes, dizziness, confu‑
sion, seizures, etc., the risk of injury should be taken into 
account. Due to the intricate mechanisms underlying 
their anti‑inflammatory and immunosuppressive actions, 
glucocorticoids (GCs), such as prednisone, hydrocortisone, 
prednisolone and dexamethasone are more potent and effec‑
tive than NSAIDs, although NSAIDs have a slightly better 
safety record (46). Weight gain, water retention, muscle weak‑
ness, diabetes, bone weakening and other long‑term adverse 
effects are associated with the use of GCs. disease modifying 
anti‑rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are pharmacological medi‑
cines that decrease autoimmune activity and delay or prevent 
joint deterioration in order to induce remission. DMARDs are 
divided into three categories as follows: Biologic DMARDs 
(bDMARDs), targeted synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs) 
and conventional synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs). 
Depending on the mechanisms through which they function, 
genetically altered protein molecules known as bDMARDs 
are categorised into multiple types, such as TNF‑α inhibi‑
tors, B‑cell depleters, B‑cell receptor inhibitors, antagonists 
of CD28 on T‑cells, IL‑1 inhibitors, IL‑6 inhibitors, IL 
12/23 inhibitor, IL‑17 inhibitors. One of the main obstacles 
preventing patients from receiving bDMARDs is the high 
cost of biologics (46‑48). Kartnig et al (49) used a novel 
ex vivo model culture system that enabled high‑content 
microscopy to characterise a palette of RA‑specific small 
compounds and biologicals with various mechanisms of 
action along with defined control stimuli. By using this 
screening approach, they were able to identify known 
RA‑related characteristics linked to certain treatments, such 
as B‑cell depletion following ex vivo rituximab treatment and 
cell‑to‑cell contact‑dependent lymphocyte activation (49). 
He et al (50) provided an overview of the possible processes 
underlying the impact of total glucosides of paeony (TGP) 
on the expression level of blood inflammatory cytokines in 
animal models of RA. Clinically, TGP tablets have been 
used extensively to treat RA with good effectiveness and 
safety records. Their research revealed that TGP can lower 
serum levels of pro‑inflammatory cytokines such as TNF‑α, 
IL‑1β, and IL‑6 and raise serum levels of anti‑inflammatory 
cytokines like IL‑10 when compared to the control group of 
the RA animal model. This has an anti‑inflammatory effect 
by controlling and enhancing inflammatory cytokine levels, 
which in turn helps to alleviate the disease (50).
If methotrexate is not contraindicated, it is advised to be the 
initial standard pharmacological therapy delivered following 
a diagnosis of RA, even though more than ten conventional 
synthetic DMARDs have been approved. Compared to other 
traditional synthetic DMARDs, it is the most effective. 
Gastrointestinal and liver issues are among the side‑effects 
associated with the use of methotrexate (51). In Japan, an 
all‑case surveillance study of 5,000 patients receiving 
infliximab over a 6‑month period found that 1,401 patients 
experienced adverse reactions, and 308 patients experienced 
severe adverse reactions. These included 108 patients with 
bacterial pneumonia, 25 with interstitial pneumonia, 22 with 
pneumocystis pneumonia and 14 with tuberculosis (52). On 
the other hand, targeted synthetic DMARDs are defined as 
inhibitors against Janus tyrosine kinase (JAKs), which are 
intracellular signalling molecules like cytokines. The drugs 
tofacitinib, baricitinib, peficitinib, upadacitinib and filgotinib 
have varying degrees of selectivity for various JAK isoforms 
and are used to treat RA. Strict screening should be followed 
prior to their use, as well as strict monitoring throughout treat‑
ment. Patients with severe infections, liver, kidney, or blood 
cell abnormalities should not use JAK inhibitors. Additionally, 
long‑term safety in terms of the development of infections such 
as herpes zoster and malignant tumours such as lymphoma 
need to be demonstrated (53‑55) (Table I).
6. Mechanisms of action of therapeutic agents
NSAIDs. The COX enzyme is inhibited by NSAIDs, which 
is their primary mode of action. Arachidonic acid must be 
converted by cyclooxygenase in order to produce prostacy‑
clins, prostaglandins, and thromboxanes. The absence of these 
eicosanoids is considered to be the cause of the therapeutic 
effects of NSAIDs. In particular, prostaglandins produce 
vasodilation, raise the hypothalamic temperature set‑point, 
and contribute to anti‑nociception, whereas thromboxanes aid 
in platelet adhesion (70). COX‑1 and COX‑2 are the two COX 
isoenzymes. The body constitutively expresses COX‑1, which 
contributes to renal function, platelet aggregation and the 
preservation of the lining of the gastrointestinal tract. COX‑2 
is inducibly expressed during an inflammatory reaction rather 
than constitutively expressed in the body. The majority of 
NSAIDs inhibit both COX‑1 and COX‑2 and are nonselec‑
tive. However, because they only target COX‑2, COX‑2 
selective NSAIDs (such celecoxib) have a different profile of 
side effects. Crucially, since COX‑2 primarily contributes to 
inflammation and COX‑1 is the primary mediator for main‑
taining the integrity of the gastric mucosa, COX‑2 selective 
NSAIDs ought to reduce inflammation without endangering 
the gastric mucosa (71).
The gastrointestinal mucosa, cardiovascular system, 
hepatic system, renal system and haematological system are 
all known to be negatively affected by NSAIDs. The inhibition 
of COX‑1, which stops the production of prostaglandins that 
shield the gastric mucosa, is probably the cause of the negative 
effects in the stomach. The reason for the negative effects on 
the kidneys is that COX‑1 and COX‑2 promote the synthesis of 
prostaglandins, which are involved in renal haemodynamics. 
Because nonselective NSAIDs have antiplatelet activity, 
haematological side‑effects are likely. Usually, this antiplatelet 
effect is only problematic if the patient has a history of GI ulcers 
or other conditions that affect platelet function. Anaphylactoid

В работе рассматриваются современные подходы к лечению ревматоидного артрита (РА), включая использование нестероидных противовоспалительных препаратов (НПВП), глюкокортикоидов (ГК) и базисных противоревматических препаратов (БПРП). НПВП, такие как ибупрофен и ингибиторы ЦОГ-2, применяются для снижения воспаления и боли, но могут вызывать серьезные побочные эффекты, включая желудочно-кишечные язвы и сердечно-сосудистые проблемы. ГК, такие как преднизон, более эффективны, но также имеют долгосрочные побочные эффекты, такие как диабет и ослабление костей.

БПРП делятся на биологические, таргетные синтетические и традиционные синтетические препараты. Биологические БПРП, такие как ингибиторы TNF-α, эффективны, но дороги. Таргетные синтетические БПРП, включая ингибиторы JAK, требуют строгого мониторинга из-за риска инфекций и опухолей. Метотрексат является стандартной терапией при РА, но может вызывать проблемы с желудочно-кишечным трактом и печенью.

Исследования показывают, что глюкозиды пиона (TGP) могут снижать уровень провоспалительных цитокинов и повышать уровень противовоспалительных, что помогает в лечении РА. Однако необходимы дополнительные исследования для подтверждения долгосрочной безопасности и эффективности этих подходов.

Основное внимание уделяется группе препаратов DMARDs, которые нарушают воспалительные каскадные пути. Метотрексат, например, подавляет клеточный иммунитет и снижает уровни IL-6 и IL-8. Лефлуномид предотвращает пролиферацию лимфоцитов, ингибируя дигидрооротатдегидрогеназу. Сульфасалазин оказывает противовоспалительное действие, ингибируя окислительное повреждение. Гидроксихлорохин блокирует внутриклеточный Toll-подобный рецептор 9. Побочные эффекты DMARDs включают диарею, сыпь и ретинопатию. В таблице представлены распространенные противоревматические препараты, их механизмы действия, год открытия и побочные эффекты. Например, метотрексат вызывает желудочно-кишечные и печеночные проблемы, а лефлуномид может привести к диарее, тошноте и печеночной недостаточности.

substances have common side‑effects, including rash or 
allergic reaction, bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, 
gastrointestinal distress (diarrhoea, nausea and stomach pain), 
and an increased risk of common and occasionally serious 
infections. Leflunomide and methotrexate can both result in 
baldness. Liver cirrhosis, folic acid deficiency, and interstitial 
lung disease are other side effects specific to methotrexate. 
Weight loss, peripheral neuropathy, and hypertension are all 
side effects of leflunomide. Gastrointestinal distress is a very 
real danger with sulfasalazine. An elevated risk of common 
and dangerous infections, such as bacterial, fungal, and viral 
infections, is the most worrisome side effect of all biologic 
DMARDs. Hepatitis B/C, herpes zoster and tuberculosis can 
also reactivate. Biologic DMARDs have infrequently been 
linked to hepatotoxicity and bone marrow suppression (74).
Corticosteroids. The biological effects of corticosteroids are 
diverse and include immunosuppressive and anti‑inflammatory 
properties. Leucocyte mobility and, to a lesser extent, leuco‑
cyte function are significantly impacted by them. Generally 
speaking, they impact cellular functions more than humoral 
ones. Prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and other metabolites of 
arachidonic acid, as well as certain cytokines such as IL‑1, are 
inhibited by these (75).
GCs a subtype of corticosteroid, use a variety of methods 
to achieve their potent immunosuppressive and anti‑inflamma‑
tory actions. Almost all primary or secondary immune cells 
are impacted by GCs at the cellular level. They interfere with 
leukocyte, fibroblast and endothelial cell activities, restrict the 
generation and effects of humoral factors, and prevent leuko‑
cyte traffic and access to the site of inflammation (76).
There are numerous potential side effects of corticosteroid 
medication. Weight gain and Cushinghoid traits, such as moon 
face, hirsutism, skin atrophy, bruises, posterior subcapsular 
cataract, mood swings, and osteoporosis, are more frequent 
side effects associated with prolonged treatment. Some of 
the negative consequences are more severe and might need to 
be watched: elevated blood glucose, particularly in diabetic 
patients, hypertension, and heightened vulnerability to infec‑
tion and avascular bone necrosis (77).
Conventional synthetic disease‑modifying antirheumatic 
medications (csDMARDs) were the first line of treatment for 
RA in the past. Biological or targeted synthetic DMARDs 
were then added. But since each patient responds differently to 
treatment, it is acknowledged that a one‑size‑fits‑all strategy is 
inadequate. By customising RA treatment according to each 
patient's distinct genetic, serological, and clinical character‑
istics, personalised medicine seeks to provide more efficient 
and focused therapeutic approaches. This change is fuelled by 
developments in machine learning, pharmacogenomics, and 
biomarker research, all of which support a more customised 
strategy for managing RA (78). In contrast to the conventional 
‘one‑size‑fits‑all’ approach, personalised medicine seeks to 
customise treatment plans for each patient. Biomarkers in 
RA assist physicians in determining which individuals are 
most likely to experience severe symptoms, predicting which 
patients will benefit from particular treatments, and reducing 
the possibility of side‑effects.
Tools such as the Simplified Disease Activity Index 
(SDAI), the Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI) and the 
Disease Activity Score in 28 Joints (DAS28) are frequently 
used to measure disease activity. As they offer a standardised, 
quantitative method of tracking the course of RA and the 
effectiveness of treatment, these tools are very helpful for 
personalised medicine. While CDAI is useful for making 
clinical choices in real time when test findings aren't imme‑
diately available, SDAI, with its CRP component, provides a 
measurement that is more sensitive to inflammation. Doctors 
can more accurately adapt therapy, such as adding biologics, 
changing dosages, or even decreasing drugs in cases of remis‑
sion, by routinely monitoring SDAI or CDAI scores.
Additionally, these indices are employed in clinical trials 
to assess the effectiveness of novel drugs and make sure that 
treatment goals (such as ‘treat‑to‑target’ tactics) are being 
reached. The objective of customising RA treatment for each 
the particular condition of each patient is advanced in practice 
by SDAI and CDAI, which aid in bridging the gap between 
clinical observations and molecular‑level insights from 
biomarkers (79).
Based on response and development, these objective 
metrics aid in directing therapy modifications. ACPAs and RF 
are two examples of serological markers that shed light on the 
prognosis and severity of the disease. Compared to RF, ACPAs 
are more specific and frequently linked to more severe forms of 
the illness. Variants in the HLA‑DRB1 gene are one example of 
a prognostic biomarker that aids in predicting the severity of the 
disease and the possibility of joint injury. The 14‑3‑3η protein 
is another new prognostic indicator that has been connected to 
accelerated disease progression. As they help determine which 
medications are most likely to be effective for a given patient, 
predictive biomarkers are essential to personalised medicine. 
For instance, the response of a patient to TNF inhibitors such 
as infliximab or adalimumab may be affected by specific poly‑
morphisms in the Fc gamma receptor gene. Serum medication 
levels and inflammatory cytokines such as IL‑6 and TNF‑α 
are examples of pharmacodynamic biomarkers that provide 
real‑time information about how a drug is functioning in the 
body. In the event that the current treatment proves ineffective, 
these biomarkers allow therapists to adjust dosages or change 
medicines (80). Additionally, by identifying patients who are 
susceptible to side effects, safety biomarkers aid in the preven‑
tion of adverse medication reactions. For instance, TPMT gene 
variations can alert against thiopurine medication toxicity, and 
liver enzyme levels are tracked throughout methotrexate treat‑
ment. Incorporating biomarkers into RA treatment expedites 
medication development while also personalising care. In 
order to increase success rates and expedite the approval of 
novel treatments, pharmaceutical companies now plan clinical 
trials that concentrate on particular patient subgroups found 
using biomarkers. Furthermore, precision medicine is being 
pushed by cutting‑edge technologies, such as AI‑driven data 
analysis and multi‑biomarker disease activity assays, which 
detect a combination of inflammatory indicators. Additionally, 
liquid biopsies, which monitor inflammatory chemicals in the 
blood, are becoming increasingly popular as real‑time disease 
monitoring methods (81).
The development of combination medicines suited to 
certain immunological profiles, the expansion of pharmacoge‑
nomic databases and the improvement of predictive algorithms 
are the main areas of ongoing research. It is anticipated that

Внедрение биомаркеров в лечение РА способствует персонализации терапии и ускоряет разработку новых лекарств.

summarization: Современное лечение ревматоидного артрита (РА) будет пересмотрено с учетом внедрения прецизионной медицины в клинические рекомендации. Усложнение заболеваний требует перехода к использованию природных источников в разработке лекарств, так как они предлагают богатый выбор фармакологически активных соединений. Синтетические фармакофоры часто не могут полностью учесть сложные взаимодействия в биологических системах, что снижает их эффективность и увеличивает побочные эффекты. Природные подходы могут открыть новые фармакофоры, которые эффективно воздействуют на сложные механизмы заболеваний. Это может революционизировать разработку лекарств, делая их более эффективными, безопасными и устойчивыми. Традиционные методы лечения РА имеют проблемы с безопасностью и эффективностью, поэтому многие пациенты обращаются к альтернативной медицине. Около 60-90% людей с артритом используют такие методы. Необходимы исследования безопасности и эффективности растительных лекарств, так как интерес к ним среди пациентов с РА растет. Лечение РА требует мультидисциплинарного подхода для снижения воспаления и облегчения боли.

restoring joint function. Herbal medicines that interact with 
inflammatory mediators have become increasingly popular in 
the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (84).
Herbal remedies are often perceived as more ‘natural’ 
compared to synthetic medications. Some individuals 
prefer herbal treatments as they feel more comfortable with 
substances derived directly from plants (85). In some cases, 
herbal remedies may be associated with fewer side‑effects 
compared to certain conventional medications. Cultural and 
traditional beliefs may influence the preference for herbal 
remedies. In some cultures, traditional herbal medicine 
has a long history of use and is deeply rooted in local prac‑
tices (86,87). They are sometimes seen as part of a holistic 
approach to health, addressing not only the symptoms but also 
focusing on overall well‑being and lifestyle changes. They may 
be more readily available and accessible to some individuals, 
particularly in regions where conventional medications may be 
less accessible or more expensive. Natural product consump‑
tion may be advantageous for RA patients in the context of 
antioxidants. Since there is currently minimal research avail‑
able in this area, there is conflicting evidence regarding the 
role of antioxidants in RA. However, the value of antioxidants 
in reducing inflammation is well‑established, which explains 
why natural products' antioxidant properties are frequently 
assessed and typically come first in vitro evaluations before 
their anti‑inflammatory properties (88).
Some herbs have been reported to have curative proper‑
ties for RA. For example, Evolvulus alsinoides (IC50 value, 
3.462 mg\ml) using aqueous solvent (89), Drynaria quercifolia 
using methanol (IC50 value, 16.90 µg) and aqueous (IC50 
value, 20.24 µg) as solvents for studying their anti‑inflam‑
matory properties (90), Alpinia galanga with hexane (IC50 
value, 800.52 µg\ml), ethyl acetate (IC50 value, 475.87 µg\
ml) and methanol (IC50 value, 364.31 µg\ml) as solvents (91), 
Kaempferia galangal with hexane (IC50 value‑831.82 µg\ml), 
ethyl acetate (IC50 value‑492.75 µg\ml) and methanol (IC50 
value‑424.44 µg\ml) as a solvents (91). Boswellia serrata 
essential oil with methanol (IC50 value‑7.514%) as a solvent 
for studying its anti‑inflammatory properties (92).
Recent studies have identified a number of herbs that 
may have therapeutic benefits for RA, providing informa‑
tion on potential future treatments. The major ingredient of 
turmeric, curcumin, has been thoroughly investigated for 
its immunomodulatory and anti‑inflammatory qualities. It 
suppresses pro‑inflammatory cytokines that are essential 
to the pathophysiology of RA, including TNF‑α, IL‑6, and 
IL‑1β by altering leukotriene pathways (93). In their review, 
Deng et al (94) revealed two distinct macrophage phenotypes: 
Classically activated M1 macrophages produce cytokines, 
chemokines, and various inflammatory agents that worsen 
inflammation, whereas alternatively activated M2 macro‑
phages reduce inflammation and promote tissue repair. 
During the development and course of RA, an imbalance in 
the M1/M2 macrophage ratio is crucial. The major ingredient 
of turmeric, curcumin, has potent immunomodulatory proper‑
ties and is used to treat a number of autoimmune conditions, 
including RA (94). Curcumin is a natural substance that helps 
RA patients with their symptoms because of its strong effec‑
tiveness, low cost and few adverse effects. Curcumin has been 
shown to have therapeutic promise in slowing the course of 
RA, which may be related to its ability to decrease macro‑
phage migration, promote macrophage polarisation towards 
the M2 phenotype and inhibit cytokines produced by M1 
macrophages (94).
Boswellia serrata, sometimes known as Indian frank‑
incense, has also been shown to lessen joint inflammation. 
Epigallocatechin gallate, one of the polyphenols found in 
green tea, has demonstrated potential in preventing oxidative 
stress and inflammation (95). Furthermore, the immuno‑
suppressive and cartilage‑protective properties of ginger, 
ashwagandha and Tripterygium wilfordii (Thunder God Vine) 
have been studied, opening up new possibilities for integra‑
tive therapy approaches. Thunder God Vine is a traditional 
Chinese medicinal herb that has strong immunosuppressive 
and anti‑inflammatory effects. RA and other autoimmune 
illnesses have been treated with it for decades. It is one of the 
most promising herbal alternatives to traditional treatment for 
RA due to recent scientific investigations into its mechanisms 
of action, therapeutic potential and clinical efficacy. It inhibits 
the synthesis of important inflammatory mediators, including 
IL‑6, IL‑1β and TNF‑α. These cytokines play a significant 
role in the inflammation and cartilage degradation linked to 
RA (96).
Triptolide and celastrol, two of the active ingredients of 
Tripterygium wilfordii, control T‑cell and B‑cell activity, 
lowering the creation of autoantibodies and inflammatory 
reactions. In particular, triptolide has been demonstrated to 
restore immunological homeostasis by promoting the expan‑
sion of regulatory T‑cells (Treg) and inhibiting Th17 cell 
development. The inhibition of the NF‑κB and JAK/STAT 
signalling pathways, which are essential for the transcription 
of inflammatory genes in the pathophysiology of RA, are the 
mechanisms through which Tripterygium wilfordii exerts its 
potent anti‑inflammatory effects. Research has shown that 
triptolide inhibits RANKL, a crucial component in the bone 
loss associated with RA, hence preventing osteoclast develop‑
ment and bone resorption (97).
Research on complementary and alternative medicine 
techniques that could improve traditional RA treatments 
is made possible by these plants. Targeting FLS, which are 
crucial in the degeneration of joints linked to RA, is one 
intriguing avenue. To specifically stop inflammatory signal‑
ling, inhibitors of particular pathways are being developed, 
such as cadherin‑11 and JAK inhibitors (98). Since dysbiosis 
has been connected to autoimmune illnesses, such as RA, 
altering the gut microbiota is another intriguing approach. 
Microbiome‑targeted treatments and probiotics may help 
control immune responses and enhance therapeutic results. 
Adaptive and precision medicine methods are changing the 
way RA treatments are studied and used in clinical trials. The 
possibility of successful treatment responses is increased by 
the classification of patients based on genetic, serological, and 
molecular profiles made possible by biomarker‑driven clinical 
trials. To guarantee a more thorough assessment of therapy 
efficacy, trial techniques are increasingly integrating wearable 
technologies, real‑world data integration, and patient‑reported 
outcomes (99).

В научной работе рассматриваются патогенез и лечение ревматоидного артрита (РА) с акцентом на использование травяных подходов. Травяные лекарства становятся популярными из-за их натурального происхождения и меньшего количества побочных эффектов по сравнению с синтетическими препаратами. В некоторых культурах травяные средства имеют долгую историю использования и считаются частью целостного подхода к здоровью.

Исследования показывают, что некоторые травы обладают лечебными свойствами для РА. Например, куркумин, основной компонент куркумы, обладает иммуномодулирующими и противовоспалительными свойствами, подавляя провоспалительные цитокины, такие как TNF-α, IL-6 и IL-1β. Boswellia serrata и полифенолы зеленого чая также демонстрируют потенциал в снижении воспаления. Иммуносупрессивные и защитные свойства имбиря, ашваганды и Tripterygium wilfordii (Громовинный виноград) открывают новые возможности для интегративной терапии.

Активные компоненты Tripterygium wilfordii, такие как триптолид и целастрол, регулируют активность Т- и В-клеток, снижая выработку аутоантител и воспалительных реакций. Эти растения открывают перспективы для улучшения традиционных методов лечения РА. Исследуются также методы, направленные на изменение микробиоты кишечника и использование пробиотиков для контроля иммунных ответов.

Адаптивные и прецизионные методы медицины меняют подходы к изучению и применению лечения РА в клинических испытаниях. Комбинированные терапии исследуют синергетические эффекты малых молекул, биологических препаратов и дополнительных терапий для оптимизации управления РА.

Latest Scientific Advancements in Rheumatoid Arthritis: A 
Comprehensive Report for Patient AI Assistant Development 
 
 
Executive Summary for AI Developers 
 
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease characterized by 
debilitating joint inflammation, pain, and progressive damage, often extending to 
various extra-articular manifestations. This report synthesizes the most current 
scientific research from 2023 to 2025, focusing on RA's complex causes, evolving 
treatment modalities, essential patient education, and the burgeoning applications of 
artificial intelligence (AI) in rheumatology. The objective is to provide a robust, 
evidence-based knowledge foundation for developing an AI assistant tailored to 
patients with RA. 
For RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system implementation, several critical 
elements emerge from this synthesis. The report highlights the multifactorial etiology 
of RA, emphasizing the interplay of genetic predispositions and environmental 
triggers.1 Treatment strategies are rapidly evolving towards personalized, 
treat-to-target approaches, with a significant focus on early intervention and the 
strategic use of advanced pharmacological agents such as Janus kinase (JAK) 
inhibitors and biologics.4 Crucially, non-pharmacological interventions and lifestyle 
modifications are presented not merely as supportive measures but as integral 
components of comprehensive patient care, directly influencing disease progression 
and symptom management.2 Furthermore, the integration of AI and machine learning 
into rheumatology is advancing rapidly, offering substantial potential for enhanced 
diagnosis, precise disease monitoring, and optimized treatment selection. This 
necessitates the AI assistant's RAG system to be built upon high-quality, structured, 
and continuously updated data to ensure effective performance and deliver current, 
evidence-based patient responses.11 The detailed information on clinical guidelines 
from leading bodies like the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and the 
European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR), alongside emerging 
therapies, is paramount for delivering authoritative and up-to-date information to

Суммаризация:

Ревматоидный артрит (РА) — это хроническое аутоиммунное заболевание, вызывающее воспаление суставов и прогрессирующее повреждение тканей. В отчете за 2023-2025 годы рассматриваются причины РА, новые методы лечения и роль искусственного интеллекта (ИИ) в ревматологии. Основное внимание уделяется многофакторной этиологии РА, включая генетические и экологические факторы. Лечение становится более персонализированным, с акцентом на раннее вмешательство и использование ингибиторов JAK и биологических препаратов. Comparative Efficacy and Safety Among JAK Inhibitors (Network Meta-Analysis): 
A comprehensive network meta-analysis comparing six JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib, 
upadacitinib, decernotinib, peficitinib, and filgotinib) provided detailed insights into their 
relative efficacy and safety.30 
●​ Efficacy Outcomes: 
○​ ACR20/50/70 Response: Decernotinib generally demonstrated the highest 
efficacy across ACR20, ACR50, and ACR70 responses. For instance, 
decernotinib showed the highest ACR20 response (RR = 2.61), ACR50 
response (RR = 5.28), and ACR70 response (RR = 6.46).30 Conversely, filgotinib

B. Key Recommendations for Treatment Strategy 
 
The major rheumatology guidelines converge on several key recommendations for the 
strategic management of RA. 
For first-line therapy, both the ACR and EULAR consistently recommend 
methotrexate, often in conjunction with short-term glucocorticoids, as the initial 
treatment strategy for RA.5 If methotrexate is contraindicated, alternatives such as 
leflunomide or sulfasalazine should be considered.6 Methotrexate monotherapy is 
strongly preferred over combination treatments for patients presenting with moderate 
to high disease activity who are new to DMARDs.5 
Regarding treatment escalation, a significant recent development highlighted by 
EULAR is the recommendation to initiate a biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD 
(b/tsDMARD) if the treatment target (remission or low disease activity) is not achieved 
with the initial conventional synthetic DMARD approach.6 This updated guidance 
removes previous requirements for patients to fail multiple csDMARDs before 
becoming eligible for b/tsDMARDs, potentially allowing for earlier access to highly 
effective therapies.6 This policy shift is particularly impactful, as it directly influences 
the speed at which patients can achieve disease control and potentially remission, 
thereby reducing the risk of irreversible joint damage and improving long-term quality 
of life. An AI assistant should highlight this accelerated pathway, emphasizing the 
importance of ongoing disease assessment and timely treatment adjustments in close 
consultation with a rheumatologist. 
Combination therapy remains a core principle; EULAR continues to recommend that 
b/tsDMARDs be combined with a csDMARD.6 However, in situations where a csDMARD 
cannot be used as a co-medication, IL-6 inhibitors and JAK inhibitors may offer 
advantages over other bDMARDs.6 
The use of corticosteroids is approached with caution in current guidelines. There is 
a strong recommendation against long-term steroid use and a conditional 
recommendation against short-term use, even as a bridge treatment, due to their 
potential for harm.5 Instead, guidelines suggest that if patients require steroids to 
reach a treatment goal, the preferred approach is to add or switch DMARDs rather 
than continuing with steroid therapy.5

IV. Patient-Centric Information and Self-Management 
 
This section provides practical, actionable advice for individuals living with RA, 
addressing common questions and concerns related to managing their condition and 
enhancing their quality of life. 
 
A. Lifestyle Modifications 
 
Rheumatology experts, such as those at NYU Langone, consistently recommend that 
patients with RA adopt specific lifestyle changes to help reduce pain and prevent 
further joint damage.7 These modifications are not merely supportive measures but 
are recognized as active therapeutic components that directly influence disease 
progression and symptom management. 
Exercise is a critical element. While the pain and stiffness of RA might deter physical 
activity, being sedentary can actually worsen symptoms.7 Regular, appropriate 
exercise helps maintain or improve joint flexibility and the strength of surrounding 
muscles, which in turn stabilizes and supports joints, preventing a cycle of worsening 
instability.7 Recommended activities include range-of-motion exercises, strength 
training, and endurance exercises such as walking, swimming, or cycling.7 Yoga and 
Pilates have also demonstrated benefits in increasing overall strength without 
overextending the joints.7 It is crucial for patients to find a balance between activity 
and rest, particularly during symptom flare-ups, allowing inflamed joints to recover.2 
Consulting a physiotherapist can provide tailored advice on suitable exercise types.8 
Diet and Nutrition play a significant role in overall wellness and weight management, 
which is particularly important for RA patients.2 Dietary habits can either exacerbate 
inflammation or offer protective benefits.10 A balanced, nutritious diet is encouraged.2

Эксперты рекомендуют пациентам с РА вносить изменения в образ жизни, чтобы уменьшить боль и предотвратить дальнейшее повреждение суставов. Физическая активность, несмотря на боль и скованность, важна для поддержания гибкости суставов и силы мышц, что стабилизирует и поддерживает суставы. Йога и пилатес также полезны для увеличения общей силы без перегрузки суставов. Важно находить баланс между активностью и отдыхом, особенно во время обострений симптомов. Питание и диета играют значительную роль в общем благополучии и управлении весом, что особенно важно для пациентов с РА. Питательные привычки могут либо усугублять воспаление, либо оказывать защитное действие. Рекомендуется сбалансированная, питательная диета, например, средиземноморская диета.

sodas have been linked to an increased risk or worsening of RA symptoms.10 Fruits, 
vegetables, olive oil, garlic, and ginger, rich in antioxidants and anti-inflammatory 
mediators, may help reduce inflammation and improve symptoms.10 
Obesity is a significant concern, as excess fatty tissue releases inflammatory 
cytokines that can exacerbate RA symptoms.2 Maintaining a moderate weight is 
therefore crucial for managing the disease and reducing the risk of associated 
comorbidities like high cholesterol, diabetes, and heart disease.2 
Alcohol intake should be limited, especially if patients are taking RA medications that 
carry a risk of liver damage. Discussion with a healthcare provider is essential to 
determine safe consumption levels.7 
Smoking cessation is strongly advised. Smoking is a known risk factor for developing 
RA and can worsen existing symptoms by promoting further inflammation.7 Quitting 
smoking has been shown to improve RA symptoms.7 
The consistent emphasis on lifestyle factors across various sources underscores that 
these elements are not merely general health recommendations but are active 
therapeutic modalities with a direct causal impact on disease activity and 
progression. An AI assistant should actively promote these lifestyle changes with the 
same emphasis as medication adherence, providing detailed, actionable guidance 
rather than generic health tips.

symptoms and improve daily comfort. 
Rest is important, particularly during symptom flare-ups, to allow inflamed joints an 
opportunity to recover.2

such as heat pads or warm baths, are effective for soothing stiff joints and tired

discomfort are complex experiences that cannot always be fully addressed by 
medication alone. Since patients may experience persistent pain and stiffness even

provide significant analgesic relief and improve quality of life, integrating these 
options into an AI assistant's advice is crucial. This approach moves beyond a purely

D. Living with RA 
 
Living with rheumatoid arthritis extends beyond managing physical symptoms; it 
encompasses significant emotional, social, and financial considerations. 
Emotional well-being is often impacted by the unpredictable nature of RA, with 
fluctuating pain, stiffness, and unexpected flare-ups.8 These challenges can 
contribute to feelings of depression, stress, and anxiety.8 It is crucial for patients to 
communicate these emotional struggles with their healthcare team, who can offer

I. Understanding Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) 
 
 
A. What is Rheumatoid Arthritis? 
 
Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease that primarily 
targets the synovial joints, leading to persistent pain, swelling, and stiffness.3 This 
condition is characterized by a progressive destruction of joint cartilage and bone 
erosions over time, which can severely impair joint function.3 RA is not confined to the 
joints; it is a systemic disorder, meaning it can extend its inflammatory effects to 
various other organs and systems throughout the body.2 
Clinically, RA is often categorized based on the duration of symptoms. "Early RA" 
refers to cases where symptoms have been present for fewer than six months, while 
"established RA" applies when symptoms have persisted for more than six months.3 
This distinction is more than just a diagnostic label; it is a critical indicator for the 
urgency of intervention. Untreated RA is a progressive disease, inevitably leading to 
increased morbidity and, in severe cases, higher mortality rates.3 The progression of 
the disease and the resulting irreversible damage underscore the profound 
importance of early and accurate diagnosis, followed by prompt initiation of 
treatment. An AI assistant designed for patients should therefore be equipped to 
recognize symptom patterns suggestive of early RA, facilitating timely medical 
consultation and emphasizing the critical need for swift intervention to mitigate 
long-term damage. 
 
B. Causes and Risk Factors 
 
The precise etiology of RA remains intricate and multifactorial, arising from a complex 
interplay of genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and immunological

For patients considering family planning, it is imperative to inform their healthcare 
team if they intend to start a family or have concerns about pregnancy while on RA 
medications. Certain drugs, including methotrexate, leflunomide, and some biologics, 
should not be taken when trying to conceive.3 The healthcare team will work 
collaboratively to ensure RA is well-controlled with pregnancy-safe options during 
conception attempts and throughout pregnancy.8 
RA can also impact sex and relationships, as pain, discomfort, and changes in 
self-esteem or body image may affect intimacy and confidence.8 While these are 
private matters, discussing their impact on sexuality and sexual relationships with a 
partner or general practitioner can be beneficial.8 
Financial considerations are a practical reality for many RA patients, especially if the 
condition necessitates stopping work or reducing to part-time employment.8 Patients 
may be eligible for various forms of financial support, including Statutory Sick Pay, 
Employment and Support Allowance, Personal Independence Payment, or Attendance 
Allowance.8 For prescriptions in England, a prescription prepayment certificate (PPC), 
which acts as a "season ticket" for prescriptions, may offer a more economical 
option.8 
Vaccinations are strongly recommended for RA patients due to their increased 
susceptibility to infections, often compounded by immunosuppressive medications. 
Patients may be advised to receive a yearly flu vaccination and a one-off 
pneumococcal vaccination to protect against serious chest infections.3 Vaccinations 
for COVID-19 and herpes zoster (shingles) are also recommended.3 
The inclusion of emotional well-being, family planning, relationship dynamics, and 
financial considerations in RA management highlights that the disease profoundly 
impacts a patient's entire life, extending far beyond purely medical symptoms. An AI 
assistant that addresses these psychosocial aspects can provide truly holistic 
support, guiding patients to relevant resources and validating their broader struggles,

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are poised to significantly 
transform the field of rheumatology, offering innovative tools to enhance diagnosis, 
optimize treatment strategies, and improve overall patient management. 
 
A. AI in Diagnosis and Disease Classification 
 
AI tools, including machine learning and deep learning, are increasingly being applied 
to analyze and interpret vast patient datasets for rheumatic diseases.11 This capability 
extends beyond simple data processing to sophisticated pattern recognition. 
For the automated identification of RA, ML and deep learning models can analyze 
various patient data points, including demographics, antibody profiles (such as 
rheumatoid factor and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies), laboratory test results, 
and radiographic images. These models have demonstrated high accuracy in 
diagnosing RA, with reported F1 scores of 0.92 and AUROC (Area Under the Receiver 
Operating Characteristic curve) values of 0.95.11 
Imaging analysis is another area where AI is making substantial inroads. 
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a specialized form of artificial neural networks, 
can diagnose RA by analyzing plain hand radiographs, identifying characteristic 
abnormalities like periarticular osteopenia and juxta-articular erosions with up to 
73.33% accuracy.11 ML models have achieved even higher accuracy, up to 90.7%, in 
distinguishing RA and osteoarthritis from normal hand radiographs.11 Beyond X-rays, 
AI is being used to analyze other imaging modalities such as MRI, CT, ultrasound, and 
thermography for diagnosis, assessment of disease activity, and detection of 
structural lesions. For instance, CNNs can differentiate RA and psoriatic arthritis 
based on hand MRIs with an AUC-ROC of 0.75.11 
AI's capabilities extend to the sub-classification of RA patients, moving beyond the 
current broad diagnostic criteria. ML applied to synovial tissue biopsies and gene 
expression analysis can define distinct synovial gene expression subtypes (e.g., high, 
low, or mixed inflammatory profiles).12 This sub-classification holds significant 
promise, as these molecular phenotypes may predict a patient's likelihood of poor 
response to certain anti-rheumatic drugs.12 Furthermore, research is integrating

The ability of AI to not only diagnose RA but also to sub-classify patients based on

predict treatment response or disease progression, it shifts the approach from 
reactive diagnosis to proactive, personalized treatment selection. This suggests a

outset, minimizing the traditional trial-and-error approach and potentially improving 
patient outcomes more rapidly. An AI assistant for patients could explain the concept

pathways. 
 
B. AI in Flare Detection and Disease Activity Monitoring 
 
AI is revolutionizing the monitoring of RA disease activity, transforming episodic 
clinical assessments into continuous, objective surveillance. 
Wearable activity trackers coupled with AI models can detect RA flares by analyzing 
patterns in physical activity data. These models have demonstrated high sensitivity 
(95.7%) and specificity (96.7%) in identifying flares.12 This capability for continuous 
monitoring allows for the proactive identification of patients experiencing high flare 
rates, enabling healthcare providers to prioritize them for earlier clinic visits and timely 
interventions.12 
Point of Care Ultrasound (POCUS) analysis is another area benefiting from deep 
learning models, particularly CNNs. These models are being applied to Doppler 
ultrasound images to accurately detect diseased synovium and score disease activity 
in RA, achieving high accuracy comparable to expert rheumatologists.12 This 
technology offers a non-invasive, real-time assessment of joint inflammation.

The application of AI to wearable data and imaging for flare detection and disease 
activity monitoring fundamentally changes how RA is managed. If flares can be 
detected proactively via wearables and joint damage objectively assessed by 
AI-powered imaging, then patients can receive timely interventions, potentially 
preventing irreversible damage and significantly improving their quality of life. This 
shifts the paradigm from reactive disease management to a more predictive and 
preventive care model, where an AI assistant could potentially alert patients to early 
signs of a flare or indicate the need for a follow-up check-up. 
 
C. AI in Treatment Choice and Outcome Prediction 
 
AI's capabilities in predicting patient responses to therapies and integrating diverse 
data sources are significantly enhancing treatment decision-making in rheumatology. 
AI models can predict which patients are most likely to respond to specific therapies, 
a crucial capability, especially in cases where first-line treatments prove ineffective.11 
These models can forecast changes in disease activity scores (DAS) and identify 
non-responders to treatments like anti-TNF therapy.12 The accuracy of these 
predictions can be further improved by combining clinical data with genomic 
biomarkers.11 
The concept of Explainable AI (XAI) is gaining traction to address the "black box" 
nature of complex AI algorithms. XAI approaches are increasingly used to provide 
transparency by elucidating the rationale behind the machine learning algorithm's 
outputs, thereby minimizing bias and fostering trust in treatment recommendations.12 
The utilization of Electronic Health Record (EHR) data by ML and deep learning 
models is proving highly valuable. By analyzing structured EHR data, AI can predict RA 
disease activity at future clinical visits with high accuracy, achieving an AUROC of 0.91 
in some test cohorts.12 This predictive power can help clinicians anticipate disease 
course and plan interventions more effectively.

D. Future Implications and Challenges 
 
Despite the immense potential of AI in rheumatology, its widespread implementation 
faces several significant challenges that require careful consideration and strategic 
solutions.

"black box" problem. Many complex deep learning algorithms provide conclusions

The rapid advancement and adoption of AI tools necessitate robust regulatory 
frameworks. Widespread clinical implementation requires high levels of regulation to 
ensure patient safety and efficacy.12 New reporting guidelines (e.g., TRIPOD-AI, 
CONSORT-AI) and regulatory frameworks (e.g., the EU’s AI Act) are actively being 
developed to address these concerns.11 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 
has also issued an ‘AI/ML-Based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) Action Plan’ to 
guide the oversight of AI tools in healthcare.12 
Clinician training and participation are also vital. The rapid integration of AI tools 
with minimal training for clinicians can limit their effective use and impact on 
diagnostic accuracy.11 Active physician participation in the development of AI models 
and the incorporation of AI elements into medical education are crucial to prepare 
future healthcare professionals for this evolving landscape.12 
Finally, ethical concerns surround AI in healthcare. Cases of unethical use, such as 
generating fraudulent research, have already led to paper retractions.11 There is also a 
significant risk of 
algorithmic bias, where flawed or non-representative training data can lead to 
skewed outcomes, potentially disadvantaging certain patient groups or perpetuating 
health inequities.11 
The challenges of data quality, interpretability, and bias highlight that the mere 
deployment of AI is insufficient; ethical considerations and robust validation are 
paramount for building patient trust and ensuring safety. If AI models are prone to 
"hallucinations" or "algorithmic bias," their direct application in patient-facing roles 
without rigorous oversight and transparency could lead to misinformation or 
inequitable care. This implies that an AI assistant must be designed with built-in 
mechanisms for accuracy verification, clear disclaimers about its role as a 
supplementary tool, and a steadfast commitment to continuous improvement based 
on real-world clinical validation and ethical guidelines.

A. Factors Influencing Prognosis 
 
The progression of RA can vary significantly among individuals, making it challenging 
to predict the exact long-term effects on a person's life expectancy.27 However, 
several factors are known to influence the prognosis. 
Early detection and treatment are paramount. Prompt diagnosis and the initiation of 
aggressive treatment regimens significantly improve a patient's quality of life and 
effectively slow disease progression.3 With appropriate and consistent treatment, 
many individuals can live well into their 80s or 90s, experiencing relatively mild 
symptoms and only minor limitations in their daily lives.27 
The disease progression itself naturally impacts the outlook. RA typically advances 
through stages characterized by increasing joint damage, pain, and restricted 
movement.27 It is estimated that approximately 40% of individuals diagnosed with RA 
may experience some degree of disability within 10 years of their diagnosis.27 
Lifestyle factors play a substantial role in influencing the long-term outlook. Smoking 
tobacco, for instance, not only acts as a significant risk factor for developing RA but 
also negatively impacts the progression of the disease by exacerbating 
inflammation.27 Similarly, 
obesity can worsen RA symptoms, as fatty tissue releases inflammatory cytokines 
that contribute to the disease process.27 Maintaining a moderate weight is therefore a 
crucial modifiable factor that can help manage symptoms.27 
The age at disease onset also affects prognosis; when RA begins at a younger age, 
there is a longer period for the disease to progress, potentially leading to more severe 
symptoms and complications over time.27 
Furthermore, the presence of comorbidities significantly impacts the long-term 
prognosis and can increase mortality.3 RA increases the risk of various associated 
conditions, including osteoporosis, rheumatoid nodules, dry eyes and mouth 
(secondary Sjögren's syndrome), infections, carpal tunnel syndrome, heart problems 
(such as hardened arteries and inflammation around the heart), lung disease

При правильной терапии многие пациенты могут дожить до 80-90 лет с минимальными симптомами. The strong correlation between early intervention, consistent adherence to treatment, 
and positive lifestyle choices with an improved long-term prognosis suggests that 
patients have significant agency in shaping their disease course. If factors like early

B. Possibility of Remission 
 
For many individuals with rheumatoid arthritis, achieving remission is a tangible and 
achievable goal, particularly when the disease is diagnosed early and treated 
promptly and aggressively.27 
Doctors define RA as being in remission based on specific clinical and laboratory 
criteria: 
●​ Swelling and tenderness should affect a maximum of one joint. 
●​ Blood tests should indicate little or no inflammation. 
●​ An overall assessment of arthritis activity should be 1 or less on a scale of 0–10.27 
Once a patient achieves sustained remission, typically maintained for at least six 
months, healthcare providers may consider tapering medications.5 While dose 
reduction or gradual discontinuation is conditionally recommended over abrupt 
cessation, guidelines generally emphasize the importance of remaining on DMARDs 
rather than stopping therapy entirely to prevent disease recurrence.5 
The explicit criteria for remission and the discussion around medication tapering in 
sustained remission transform remission from a distant hope into a concrete, 
measurable objective that is achievable for many patients. If remission is clearly 
defined and attainable, particularly with early and aggressive treatment, then an AI 
assistant can provide a more optimistic and goal-oriented perspective. This helps 
manage patient expectations realistically while simultaneously motivating adherence 
to treatment plans, as the possibility of reducing medication is a strong incentive for

Conclusions 
 
This comprehensive report highlights the dynamic and evolving landscape of 
rheumatoid arthritis, from its complex multifactorial origins to the latest 
advancements in its management. For the development of an AI assistant for RA 
patients, several key conclusions and recommendations emerge: 
1.​ Emphasize Early Intervention and Personalized Care: RA is a progressive 
disease where early diagnosis and prompt, aggressive treatment are critical to 
prevent irreversible joint damage and improve long-term outcomes. The AI 
assistant should be designed to recognize early symptom patterns and guide 
users towards timely medical consultation. Furthermore, the shift towards a 
"Treat-to-Target" approach and the nuanced risk-benefit profiles of advanced 
therapies underscore the importance of personalized treatment plans. The AI 
should facilitate patient understanding of this collaborative goal-setting and how 
individual data informs therapeutic choices. 
2.​ Integrate Holistic Management Strategies: RA is a systemic condition affecting 
multiple organs and impacting various aspects of a patient's life, including 
emotional, social, and financial well-being. The AI assistant must provide 
comprehensive information that extends beyond pharmacological treatments to 
include crucial lifestyle modifications (diet, exercise, smoking cessation), 
non-pharmacological symptom management techniques (hot/cold therapy, stress 
reduction), and psychosocial support resources. This holistic approach will 
empower patients to take an active role in their self-management and address 
the broader challenges of living with a chronic illness. 
3.​ Prioritize Current and Comparative Treatment Information: The rapid 
evolution of pharmacological therapies, including the introduction of new JAK 
inhibitors, biologics, and biosimilars, necessitates that the AI assistant's 
knowledge base is continuously updated. The AI should be capable of providing 
detailed, comparative information on the efficacy and safety of different 
treatment options, allowing patients to understand the rationale behind their 
prescribed therapies and engage in informed discussions with their healthcare 
providers. The availability of biosimilars particularly warrants highlighting their 
role in improving accessibility to advanced treatments.

Этот отчет подчеркивает сложный и изменяющийся характер ревматоидного артрита (РА), от его многофакторных причин до последних достижений в лечении. Для разработки AI-ассистента для пациентов с РА выделены ключевые рекомендации:

1. Ранняя интервенция и персонализированный подход: РА — прогрессирующее заболевание, где ранняя диагностика и агрессивное лечение важны для предотвращения необратимых повреждений суставов и улучшения долгосрочных результатов. AI-ассистент должен распознавать ранние симптомы и направлять пользователей к своевременной медицинской консультации, а также поддерживать персонализированные планы лечения.

2. Интеграция холистических стратегий управления: РА влияет на различные аспекты жизни пациента. AI-ассистент должен предоставлять информацию не только о медикаментозном лечении, но и о важных изменениях образа жизни, методах немедикаментозного управления симптомами и ресурсах психосоциальной поддержки.

3. Актуальная информация о лечении: Быстрое развитие фармакологических терапий требует постоянного обновления базы знаний AI-ассистента. Он должен предоставлять сравнительную информацию об эффективности и безопасности различных вариантов лечения, включая роль биосимиляров в улучшении доступности передовых терапий.

Genetic factors play a substantial role in determining an individual's susceptibility to 
RA. A higher incidence of RA is observed within families, with first-degree relatives 
carrying the greatest risk, contributing to an estimated 40-50% of seropositive RA 
cases.1 Among the most potent genetic risk factors are specific alleles within the 
Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC), particularly HLA-DRB1 alleles (such as DR4 
and DR1). These alleles encode a distinctive amino acid sequence known as the 
"shared epitope" (SE), which has a well-established association with anti-citrullinated 
protein antibody (ACPA)-positive RA.1 Beyond HLA-DRB1, other HLA class I and II 
genes (HLA-A and HLA-DPB1) are also independently linked to RA susceptibility.1 
Environmental triggers are believed to activate these genetic predispositions in 
susceptible individuals. Prominent among these triggers is smoking, which is a 
significant risk factor for RA development and can exacerbate disease progression by 
promoting further inflammation.3 Exposure to secondhand smoke during childhood 
has also been associated with an increased risk of RA.27 Other suspected 
environmental factors include certain viruses or bacteria, as well as physical or 
emotional stress, which can potentially initiate the autoimmune cascade.2 Diet and 
nutrition also hold a notable position as environmental modifiers. While excessive 
consumption of red meat, high dietary sodium, and sugar-sweetened sodas has been 
linked to an increased risk or worsening of RA, a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, olive oil, 
garlic, and ginger may offer protective benefits due to their antioxidant and 
anti-inflammatory properties.10 
At the core of RA pathogenesis is immune system dysregulation. In healthy individuals, 
the immune system defends against foreign invaders; however, in RA, it erroneously 
identifies the body's own tissues, particularly the synovium, as threats.2 This leads to 
the release of inflammatory chemicals that attack these self-tissues.2 This 
autoimmune response, often initiated by environmental factors in genetically 
predisposed individuals, can commence at sites distant from the synovial joints, such 
as the lungs or gums. In these peripheral tissues, biochemical reactions like 
citrullination modify proteins, generating "neoantigens" that then trigger an immune 
response and the formation of autoantibodies.3 The dysregulation of citrullination is 
directly linked to the generation of ACPAs, which are found in 60-70% of RA patients.1 
Rheumatoid factor (RF) is another well-known autoantibody, and the presence of 
either defines "seropositive RA".1 Additionally, anti-carbamylated protein antibodies 
(anti-CarP antibodies), distinct from ACPAs, are also observed in RA patients.3

Генетические факторы играют значительную роль в предрасположенности к ревматоидному артриту (РА). В семьях наблюдается более высокая частота РА, особенно среди близких родственников, что составляет 40-50% серопозитивных случаев РА. Ключевыми генетическими факторами риска являются аллели в главном комплексе гистосовместимости (MHC), особенно HLA-DRB1 (например, DR4 и DR1), связанные с анти-цитруллинированными белковыми антителами (ACPA)-положительным РА. Другие гены HLA (HLA-A и HLA-DPB1) также связаны с предрасположенностью к РА.

Экологические факторы могут активировать генетическую предрасположенность. Курение является значительным фактором риска развития РА и может усугублять течение болезни. Также риск увеличивается при воздействии пассивного курения в детстве. Другие возможные факторы включают вирусы, бактерии, физический или эмоциональный стресс. Питание также влияет на риск РА: избыток красного мяса, натрия и сладких напитков увеличивает риск, тогда как диета, богатая фруктами, овощами, оливковым маслом, чесноком и имбирем, может иметь защитный эффект.

В основе патогенеза РА лежит дисрегуляция иммунной системы, которая ошибочно атакует собственные ткани организма, особенно синовиальную оболочку. Это приводит к воспалению и образованию аутоантител, таких как ACPA и ревматоидный фактор (RF), которые определяют "серопозитивный РА". Также у пациентов с РА наблюдаются антитела к карбамилированным белкам (anti-CarP).

4.​ Educate on the Role and Limitations of AI in Healthcare: The report 
demonstrates AI's transformative potential in RA diagnosis, disease monitoring 
(e.g., flare detection via wearables), and treatment prediction. The AI assistant 
can explain how these technologies contribute to precision medicine and 
proactive care. Simultaneously, it is crucial to transparently communicate the 
current limitations of AI, such as the "black box" problem, potential for 
algorithmic bias, and the need for robust regulatory oversight. The AI assistant 
should always present itself as a supplementary tool, emphasizing that medical 
decisions must be made in consultation with qualified healthcare professionals. 
5.​ Foster Patient Empowerment and Adherence: By clearly explaining the 
dynamic nature of RA management, the purpose of regular monitoring (e.g., DAS 
scores), and the possibility of achieving and maintaining remission, the AI 
assistant can empower patients. It should reinforce the critical importance of 
medication adherence, regular medical reviews, and proactive self-care as key 
drivers for achieving positive long-term prognoses and potentially reaching 
remission. 
By adhering to these principles, the AI assistant can serve as a highly valuable, 
evidence-based resource, supporting patients with rheumatoid arthritis in navigating 
their condition, making informed decisions, and improving their overall quality of life.
